newsitem.title: ITALY: League's Bossi threatens tax strike over N.Italy.
newsitem.headline: League's Bossi threatens tax strike over N.Italy.

text.p: Umberto Bossi, firebrand leader of Italy's Northern League, threatened on Sunday to organise a tax strike unless the country's political establishment recognised what he said was the north's right to independence.

Bossi said that if Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Massimo D'Alema, leader of the biggest party in the government coalition, refused to accept the self-styled northern region of Padania's right to declare independence, "we will be forced to order a tax strike".

Bossi's remarks, made in a rousing speech winding up a three-day party congress in a convention centre in Milan, are among the most provocative he has made since espousing full-blooded separatism last year.
Prodi warned the separatist leader that the government would enforce the law.
"In a civil country, the first duty is respect for the law. The Italian government will see to it that it is respected," Prodi told reporters who asked about Bossi's threat.

The League is organising a referendum in April to test support for Bossi's proposal to create a breakaway northern state. Recent opinion polls have shown only scant support among north Italians for the cause of separatism.
"If there is no clarification of a very serious declaration by Prodi, according to which no referendum can free Padania, we will be forced to react," said Bossi.
D'Alema, leader of the post-communist PDS party, is chairman of a newly-formed parliamentary commission with a brief to draw up proposals on constitutional reform.
Bossi has pulled the League's representatives out of the commission on the grounds that it is not prepared to accept any discussion of a breakup of the Italian state.
The unity and "indivisibility" of the Italian nation is enshrined in the constitution. Italy's penal code also states that it is a crime to undermine national unity.
Earlier delegates at the party congress had voted by a wide majority to accept that the League should shun alliances with other political parties in forthcoming local elections.
Enzo Erminio Boso, a League senator, told Reuters that he gave little credit to recent opinion polls showing only limited support for a breakaway state in the north.
"Over the past six years the League has repeatedly been given up for dead," Boso said. "How can anyone be expected to believe the opinion polls of the state-controlled media?"

But his optimism did not appear to be entirely shared by Bossi, who acknowledged in a speech to the party faithful on Saturday that conditions might not yet be ripe for the north to cut loose from the rest of the country.
"If secession arrives in a society which is not yet mature it ends up badly," Bossi said, although he has shown no sign of wanting to abandon his separatist agenda.

Calls by Bossi and other League leaders for an independent state brought an immediate rejoinder on Saturday from Prodi who said the cause of separatism could prosper if Italy failed to join a single European currency.

Prodi hopes membership in a European Union single currency and sweeping institutional reform can undercut support for the League, which rose to prominence on public disgust with political corruption and a crushing tax burden.
The League won more than 10 percent of the national vote in a general election last April on a federalist platform fashioned to appeal to Italians in the affluent north.
